Mautic Twig SSTI RCE: PHP/web process spawns OS shell (CVE-2026-9558) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation observable of CVE-2026-9558 — a Mautic web-tier process (php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd/nginx worker, or w3wp) directly spawning an interactive shell or recon binary. In a healthy Mautic install the PHP runtime never forks /bin/sh or whoami; when it does, an uploaded Twig theme has broken the sandbox and reached OS-command execution. Rationale: Grounded in Mautic's confirmed PHP/Symfony/Twig stack (advisory + GitLab/NVD) — the vuln renders theme Twig without a sandbox, so successful exploitation manifests as the PHP runtime forking a shell, which never happens in a benign Mautic web request. Parent(php/apache/nginx/w3wp)->child(shell/recon) is the highest-fidelity RCE pivot available without article-supplied hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-9558 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9558/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/mautic-critical-ssti-cve-2026-9558-allows-rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mautic scheduled tasks (php bin/console mautic:segments:update / mautic:emails:send) spawning sh for symfony process helpers
  • Composer/deployment scripts run as the web user invoking shell hooks during an upgrade
  • PDF/preview generation plugins shelling out to wkhtmltopdf or imagemagick's convert
  • Admin using a web-based file manager or terminal plugin on the same PHP-FPM pool
  • Monitoring/backup agents that exec via the PHP-FPM worker (e.g. New Relic, healthcheck shellouts)
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has "bin/console" or ChildCmd has_any ("wkhtmltopdf","wkhtmltoimage","convert -","composer") or ParentCmd has "bin/console")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd — a legit Symfony console task references 'bin/console'; an attacker command runs whoami/id/curl to an external host or reads /etc/passwd or Mautic's app/config/local.php. Confirm the acting host runs Mautic and check its version against 7.1.2/6.0.9/5.2.11/4.4.20. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke sessions/API tokens for any Mautic user holding core:themes:create; block outbound to any C2 seen in the child cmdline. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for UC2 (new .twig under themes/), review Mautic audit log for recent theme installs, and sweep for dropped web shells or cron persistence written by the PHP user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "php" or ParentProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","cmd.exe","powershell","whoami","/id","uname","curl","wget","python","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mautic Twig SSTI RCE - Web Process Spawns OS Shell (CVE-2026-9558)
id: 6b2e1c9a-4f3d-4a17-9c2e-7d8f1a0b3e21
description: Detects a Mautic PHP/web-server process spawning an interactive shell or recon binary, the post-exploitation signature of the Twig theme-template SSTI in CVE-2026-9558.
references:
  - https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-9558

tags:

  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.execution
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php'
      - 'php-cgi.exe'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/nginx'
      - 'w3wp.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/id'
      - '/uname'
      - '/curl'

  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\php-cgi.exe OR *\PHP-CGI.EXE OR *\php.exe OR *\PHP.EXE OR *\php-fpm.exe OR *\w3wp.exe OR *\W3WP.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\net.exe OR *\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(php-fpm|php|php-cgi\.exe|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp\.exe)/i
| ImageFileName=/([\/](sh|bash|dash|whoami|id|uname|curl|wget|python[23]?|perl)|[\\](cmd|powershell)\.exe)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.parent_process_name="php*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="httpd" OR Processes.parent_process_name="apache2" OR Processes.parent_process_name="nginx" OR Processes.parent_process_name="w3wp.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Weaponized Twig theme written under Mautic themes/ by web process (CVE-2026-9558) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the delivery step of CVE-2026-9558 — the Mautic web tier (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) writing a .twig template into the themes/ directory, i.e. an uploaded/created theme landing on disk. Pairs with the RCE detection: a fresh web-written theme template followed by a PHP-spawned shell on the same host is the full SSTI chain. Rationale: Mautic docs confirm themes are self-contained dirs under themes/ holding *.html.twig files, installed by uploading a zip through the web UI — so the payload physically lands as a web-process-written .twig. Scoping the writer to the PHP/web runtime (not an admin's editor) separates exploit-driven writes from developer file edits and gives a clean pivot to correlate with the UC1 shell spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mautic/mautic/security/advisories/GHSA-9fx4-7cmj-47vg • https://docs.mautic.org/en/5.2/builders/creating_themes.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mautic/core/CVE-2026-9558/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator installing or updating a theme zip via Settings > Themes
  • Mautic version upgrade repopulating bundled themes (blank, cards, nature, etc.) into themes/
  • Marketing/design team uploading a custom corporate email/page theme
  • CI/CD or deployment automation syncing theme directories as the web user
  • Theme builder saving edits to email.html.twig / page.html.twig from the UI
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which Mautic user triggered the write via the app audit log (Settings > Audit Log) and correlate the timestamp with the FolderPath; a new theme folder name you don't recognize, or a modified base/page/email .twig on an internet-facing host, is suspicious. Grab and read the .twig content for SSTI markers (_self.env, registerUndefinedFilterCallback, getFilter, system/exec/passthru/proc_open). 2) Contain: quarantine the theme file, revoke core:themes:create from the acting user pending review, and confirm the host is on a patched build (7.1.2/6.0.9/5.2.11/4.4.20). 3) Hunt: run UC1 on the same DeviceName for a php-spawned shell within minutes of the write, and review web/access logs for the theme-install POST and subsequent theme-preview/render requests.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/themes/" and FileName endswith ".twig"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "php" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/themes/" and TargetFileName endswith ".twig"
| where ActingProcessName has "php" or ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Affected zebrad (<= v4.4.1) exposure to P2SH sigop consensus-split (CVE-2026-52735) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts with an installed Zebra/zebrad build at or below v4.4.1, which undercounts P2SH sigops and can be forced into a chain split from zcashd. This is asset-exposure hunting: identify vulnerable Zcash full nodes before an attacker broadcasts malicious P2SH-spend transactions. Rationale: Uses the concrete affected boundary from the advisory (zebrad <= v4.4.1, patched in 4.4.2) and CVE-2026-52735. parse_version gives an exact vulnerable-version test; SoftwareName 'zebrad' avoids collision with unrelated Zebra Technologies printer software. Note: GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 later found the 4.4.2 fix incomplete, so 4.5.1 is the true-safe floor. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gf9r-m956-97qx • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-1-security-fixes/ • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 • https://dailycve.com/zebra-consensus-divergence-critical/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Zebra Technologies label-printer / barcode driver software matching the 'zebra' string (mitigated by SoftwareName 'zebrad' filter)
  • Decommissioned or lab-only Zcash test nodes that never touch mainnet consensus
  • Host already upgraded but vuln scanner holding a stale software-inventory record
  • Vulnerability scanner mis-mapping a different Zebra advisory to this CVE
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVendor !has "Zebra Technologies" and SoftwareName !has "printer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually runs a validating full node (not just an installed binary) and note the exact SoftwareVersion — anything < 4.4.2 is exposed to CVE-2026-52735. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to a patched build; because the 4.4.2 fix was found incomplete (GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443), upgrade straight to >= 4.5.1. Until patched, monitor the node's chain tip against a reference zcashd node for divergence. 3) Hunt: enumerate all zebrad hosts via inventory, and pivot to UC 'zebrad node process execution' and the 'bad-blk-sigops' log hunt to see whether an exploit block was already accepted.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "zebrad" or (SoftwareVendor has "Zcash" and SoftwareName has "zebra")
| where isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
| where parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")   // 4.4.2 = first patched build per CVE-2026-52735
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-52735" or (SoftwareName has "zebrad" and parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-52735" OR (Vulnerabilities.signature="*zebra*" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="*sigop*") by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve | `drop_dm_object_name("Vulnerabilities")` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
zebrad node process execution at vulnerable version (CVE-2026-52735) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts live execution of the zebrad binary and surfaces its product version so analysts can confirm exposure to the P2SH sigop-undercount consensus split. Complements inventory-based detection by catching nodes launched from non-packaged paths (source builds, containers) that TVM may miss. Rationale: Anchors on the exact binary name 'zebrad' from the advisory and surfaces ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion so analysts can read the version off Windows builds; Linux builds (no version info) are still surfaced rather than dropped. Distinct pivot from the TVM inventory UC — catches source/container launches inventory misses. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gf9r-m956-97qx • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-1-security-fixes/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate zebrad node operators running an already-patched build (>= 4.5.1) — version column disambiguates on Windows
  • CI/CD or automated test harnesses repeatedly spawning zebrad
  • Container orchestration restarting zebrad pods (high event volume, benign)
  • Linux hosts where product-version metadata is empty, forcing manual version confirmation
Suppression filter
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) or parse_version(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion; if empty (typical on Linux), query the node RPC/`zebrad --version` to get the build. Versions < 4.4.2 are exposed. 2) Contain: for exposed validating nodes, plan upgrade to >= 4.5.1 (the 4.4.2 patch was incomplete) and watch the chain tip vs a reference zcashd. 3) Hunt: for every host seen running zebrad, run the 'bad-blk-sigops' log-reject hunt and cross-check the inventory UC to build the full affected-asset list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "zebrad" or FileName =~ "zebrad.exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) or parse_version(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion) < parse_version("4.4.2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "zebrad"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS infrastructure contact (pamconj.com panel + Cloudflare Worker lure) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network connections to the specific ARToken operator-panel and phishing-lure domains published by Talos (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). A host resolving/connecting to these means a user reached the device-code phishing lure or operator infrastructure — the earliest on-wire signal of this M365 token-theft campaign. Rationale: Uses the three concrete Talos-published IOC domains plus the pamconj.com apex to catch sibling operator subdomains. These are dedicated malicious infrastructure, so any resolution is high-fidelity; cross-checked against Talos, Sekoia and Microsoft reporting of the same EvilTokens/ARToken infra. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/01/eviltokens-device-code-phishing-kit-totally-more-evil-than-we-all-thought/5265409
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating the lure URL in a sandbox/SOAR enrichment from a corporate endpoint
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing to pamconj.com during investigation
  • Web proxy/URL-scanner appliance pre-fetching the domain for categorization
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ appliance logging the blocked query (benign but noisy)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/device and confirm whether the connection was a live browser navigation (device-code lure) vs automated scanner; pull the referring email/Teams message for the same recipient. 2) Contain: block all *.pamconj.com and the workers.dev lure at proxy/DNS; if a real user reached the device-code page, revoke that user's refresh tokens/sessions (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken) and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (new Entra device registration for that user) and UC3 (inbox-rule creation) within 24h; review that user's SigninLogs for device-code grants from unfamiliar IPs.

Entra ID device registration = ARToken PRT persistence after device-code token theft AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens persistence step: after stealing a refresh token via device-code phishing, the operator registers a new device in Entra ID to obtain a Primary Refresh Token for durable SSO that survives password resets. Surfaces device add/register/join audit events with the acting user, source IP and target device for rapid correlation to a suspicious sign-in. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'Primary Refresh Token (PRT) persistence' capability and corroborated by Sekoia/Microsoft describing refresh-token-driven device registration in Entra ID. Device add/register audit operations are the concrete, queryable footprint of that step; Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because Entra ID audit isn't in FDR or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/microsoft-365-phishing-panel-uses-oauth-device-code-flow/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user enrolling a new phone/laptop into Intune/Entra (BYOD or refresh cycle)
  • Autopilot/Intune bulk device provisioning by IT during onboarding
  • Windows Hello for Business device registration on password change
  • Service desk registering a replacement device for a user
Suppression filter
| where ActorIp !in ("<intune_provisioning_egress_ip>")  // NOTE: replace only if you maintain a known Intune egress allowlist; otherwise correlate ActorIp against SigninLogs device-code/foreign-IP sign-ins
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each registration confirm the actor UPN, source IP and device name; check whether the user's most recent sign-in was a device-code grant or came from an unfamiliar/foreign IP within the prior hour. 2) Contain: if unattributable, disable/remove the newly registered device, revoke the user's refresh tokens and PRTs (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken + session invalidation), and require MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: enumerate all devices registered by the same actor IP across the tenant, review SharePoint/OneDrive mass-download and inbox-rule creation (UC3) for the affected mailbox.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device","Register device","Add device")
| extend Ip = tostring(IPAddress)
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Ip, CountryCode, City, ObjectName, ObjectType
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device","Register device","Add device","Update device")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend TargetDevice = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, TargetDevice, Result, ResultReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken BEC toolkit: inbox forwarding/hiding rule creation on compromised M365 mailbox AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens post-compromise BEC action: automated creation of inbox rules that forward/redirect mail externally and delete or move messages to hide attacker activity. Targets mailbox audit events for New/Set-InboxRule carrying forwarding or delete/move parameters. Rationale: Directly targets ARToken's documented BEC capability ('inbox rule creation for forwarding and deleting messages') via the exact Exchange audit operations and forwarding/delete parameters. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because M365 mailbox audit isn't shipped to those platforms in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberscoop.com/artoken-bec-platform-cisco-talos/ • https://gbhackers.com/eviltokens-linked-artoken-panel/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately setting up out-of-office/auto-forward to a personal or delegate mailbox
  • Admin-configured transport/journaling rule mistaken for a user inbox rule
  • Power-user creating a 'move to folder' organization rule for newsletters
  • Migration tooling recreating rules during a mailbox move
Suppression filter
| where Params !has "@yourcorpdomain.com"  // keep only rules forwarding/redirecting OUTSIDE the org; internal delegate forwarding is common and low-risk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the rule forwards/redirects to an EXTERNAL domain or deletes/moves security-alert mail; check the ClientIP/country against the user's normal sign-in pattern and recent device-code sign-ins. 2) Contain: delete the malicious rule, revoke the user's tokens and PRTs, reset credentials, and block the external forwarding destination at the mail gateway. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (infra contact) and UC2 (new device registration) for the same user; search for identical rule names/forwarding targets across other mailboxes to scope the BEC blast radius.

| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity

| where Params has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated write/read to mcp-memory-service /api/documents/* endpoints (CVE-2026-50027) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP 200 responses to the unauthenticated document-API routes (upload, batch-upload, search-content, history) on a mcp-memory-service HTTP server, where the request carried no Authorization header. This is the confidentiality/integrity half of the auth-bypass: memory poisoning via upload and stored-content disclosure via search-content/history. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vulnerable route prefixes named at documents.py source lines (upload:149, search-content:729, history) plus HTTP 200; ImWebSession's HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization lets us assert the request was truly unauthenticated, which is the article's core inconsistency (/api/memories 401 vs /api/documents 200). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84hp-mqvj-3p8h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mcp-memory-service/CVE-2026-50027/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator deployed the HTTP server WITHOUT MCP_API_KEY/OAuth enabled, so legitimate clients also send no Authorization header
  • Internal ingestion/backup automation that bulk-uploads documents via the same API
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing the documented CVE route
  • The operator's own PoC/pen-test traffic against 127.0.0.1
  • Health-check or uptime probes hitting /api/documents/history
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "127." and SrcIpAddr != "::1"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull all SrcIpAddr hitting /api/documents/* with empty Authorization; confirm the server was launched with MCP_API_KEY/OAuth set (grep env of the memory server --http process). If auth was enabled, every unauthenticated 200 is a real bypass. 2) CONTAIN: Put the service behind the reverse proxy's auth or a WAF rule denying /api/documents/* without a valid bearer, and upgrade mcp-memory-service to >=10.67.1. 3) HUNT: For each attacker IP, correlate preceding /api/memories 401s and following DELETE /api/documents/remove-by-tags; review search-content/{upload_id} responses for exfiltrated memory content and inspect newly uploaded documents for prompt-injection payloads.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "/api/documents/"
| where Url has_any ("/upload", "/batch-upload", "/search-content/", "/history")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no API key / OAuth bearer supplied = the CVE-2026-50027 bypass
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "127."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mcp-memory-service auth-bypass fingerprint: /api/memories 401 then /api/documents 200 from same source AIExploitation High
Correlates the CVE-2026-50027 PoC signature on a single source IP: a 401 on the correctly-protected /api/memories endpoint followed within the hour by a successful (200) request to a /api/documents/* route with no credentials. This two-event shape is far higher fidelity than either request alone because it captures an attacker discovering the inconsistent auth boundary and pivoting to the unprotected router. Rationale: Directly models the PoC attack chain (STEP 1 GET /api/memories -> 401, STEP 4/5 POST/DELETE /api/documents/* -> 200) as a same-source temporal correlation; the 401-then-200 pairing is the article's own proof that the attacker found and exploited the inconsistent auth boundary, making it very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84hp-mqvj-3p8h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mcp-memory-service/CVE-2026-50027/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A misconfigured legitimate client whose token expired (401 on /api/memories) while a separate unauthenticated automation happens to hit /api/documents from the same NAT egress IP
  • Security scanner walking every route and recording both a 401 and a 200 from one host
  • Shared corporate proxy/NAT collapsing many users behind one SrcIpAddr
  • Operator testing both endpoints during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source IP is not a known internal proxy/scanner; inspect the exact /api/documents route that returned 200 (upload = poisoning, search-content = read, remove* = destruction). 2) CONTAIN: Block the source at the WAF/reverse proxy, disable the /api/documents/* router or gate it behind auth, and upgrade to mcp-memory-service >=10.67.1. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every upload_id this IP created or deleted; snapshot current memory store contents, diff against last known-good backup, and purge attacker-injected documents to prevent downstream prompt-injection of the AI agent.
let window = 1h;
let probes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where Url has "/api/memories" and HttpStatusCode == 401
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "/api/documents/" and HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| join kind=inner probes on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ProbeTime .. ProbeTime + window)
| project ProbeTime, BypassTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url
| order by BypassTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/memories*" OR Web.url="*/api/documents/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval memories_401=if(like(url,"%/api/memories%") AND status=401, count, 0)
| eval docs_bypass=if(like(url,"%/api/documents/%") AND status=200, count, 0)
| stats sum(memories_401) as memories_401, sum(docs_bypass) as docs_bypass, values(url) as urls, values(dest) as dest, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime by src
| where memories_401 > 0 AND docs_bypass > 0
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

Unauthenticated mass memory deletion via mcp-memory-service DELETE /api/documents/remove-by-tags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful (200) DELETE requests to the unauthenticated /api/documents/remove-by-tags and /api/documents/remove/{upload_id} routes — the availability/integrity impact of CVE-2026-50027 where an attacker permanently destroys memories belonging to authenticated users without credentials. A burst of such DELETEs from one source is a destruction event. Rationale: Uses the specific destructive routes and sink named in the article (remove-by-tags -> storage.delete_by_tags at line 705, remove/{upload_id}) constrained to DELETE + 200; a successful unauthenticated DELETE to these paths is by definition the CVE's availability impact (STEP 5 memories_deleted=1) with essentially no benign equivalent when auth is enabled. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84hp-mqvj-3p8h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mcp-memory-service/CVE-2026-50027/
ATT&CKT1485 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin housekeeping that prunes documents by tag through the same API
  • Automated retention/cleanup job deleting expired memories
  • Operator running the published PoC (tag cve-poc) during validation
  • Server started without MCP_API_KEY so all DELETEs are legitimately unauthenticated
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "127." and SrcIpAddr != "::1"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the DELETEs are unauthenticated (empty Authorization) and the server was configured with auth; count how many upload_ids/tags were removed and from which SrcIpAddr. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately block the source, take the HTTP server offline or gate /api/documents/* behind auth, upgrade to >=10.67.1, and freeze the storage backend for forensic capture before it is overwritten. 3) HUNT: Restore deleted memories from the most recent backup, diff to quantify loss, and pivot on the same IP for prior upload (poisoning) and search-content (exfiltration) calls to scope the full read/write/delete blast radius.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE"
| where Url has_any ("/api/documents/remove-by-tags", "/api/documents/remove/")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| summarize DeleteCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Urls = make_set(Url, 20) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by DeleteCount desc

PurpleFox fileless infection: remote MSI via msiexec + reflective PE injection AIInstallation High
Hunts PurpleFox's installation stage where msiexec.exe pulls a remotely hosted MSI (often disguised with a .png/.jpg/.moe extension) and installs it silently. Article-specific because the Kaspersky case study calls out an in-memory PurpleFox infection that evaded conventional EPP; the msiexec-from-URL primitive is the reliable disk-touching moment before it goes fileless. Rationale: Uses PurpleFox's documented install primitive: msiexec pulling a remote MSI with a fake .png/.jpg/.moe extension and /Q silent flag (Trend Micro, Akamai). Combination of remote URL + silent + image-extension MSI is high-fidelity and rarely legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/19/i/purple-fox-fileless-malware-with-rookit-component-delivered-by-rig-exploit-kit-now-abuses-powershell.html • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security/purple-fox-rootkit-now-propagates-as-a-worm
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1105 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software-deployment tools that fetch MSIs over HTTP(S) from an internal repo
  • SCCM/Intune win32 app installs referencing http content-delivery URLs
  • Developer/admin manually testing a hosted MSI package
  • Chocolatey/winget package installs that proxy through msiexec with a URL
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","choco.exe","winget.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("internal",".corp",".local"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full msiexec command line and the resolved URL/host; check the parent process (PurpleFox parents are often powershell.exe or a fake-image loader) and whether the fetched file has an image extension but MSI magic bytes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the download URL/IP at proxy, and capture memory before reboot (payload is fileless post-install). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for a newly created service named AC0[0-9], registry rootkit hiding, and outbound WebSocket/HTTP C2 to the same infrastructure across other endpoints.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/q","/quiet","-q")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".png",".jpg",".gif",".moe",".msi")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/q","/quiet")
| where CommandLine has_any (".png",".jpg",".gif",".moe",".msi")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PurpleFox persistence via auto-generated AC0[0-9] Windows service AIInstallation High
Hunts PurpleFox's persistence mechanism: a service whose name matches the pattern AC0 followed by a single digit (AC00–AC09), created to re-fetch/re-execute the MSI loader. Article-specific to the in-memory PurpleFox case study; the service naming convention is a durable, documented PurpleFox artifact. Rationale: PurpleFox creates a service whose name matches the regex AC0[0-9] to re-run its MSI installer (Trend Micro). Enumerating AC00–AC09 keeps queries executable with no placeholders and is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/19/i/purple-fox-fileless-malware-with-rookit-component-delivered-by-rig-exploit-kit-now-abuses-powershell.html
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate vendor service coincidentally named AC00-AC09 (rare; verify ImagePath/signature)
  • Custom in-house tooling using AC0-prefixed short names
  • Security-tool test artifacts left in a lab image
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the service ImagePath (ServiceFileName / RegStringValue) — PurpleFox points to a rundll32/msiexec or for-loop URL iterator; verify signature and file presence. 2) Contain: stop and delete the service, isolate the host, snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: search the estate for other AC0x services and for the msiexec-remote-MSI behaviour (UC1) tied to the same C2 to scope PurpleFox spread.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryKeyCreated"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\AC00",@"\Services\AC01",@"\Services\AC02",@"\Services\AC03",@"\Services\AC04",@"\Services\AC05",@"\Services\AC06",@"\Services\AC07",@"\Services\AC08",@"\Services\AC09")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName in~ ("AC00","AC01","AC02","AC03","AC04","AC05","AC06","AC07","AC08","AC09")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LionTail backdoor: DLL search-order hijack via phantom System32 DLLs AIInstallation High
Hunts installation of the LionTail (Scarred Manticore / Iran MOIS) passive backdoor, which is dropped into C:\Windows\System32 as commonly-absent 'phantom' DLLs (wlanapi.dll, wlbsctrl.dll, TSMSISrv.dll, TSVIPSrv.dll) to be side-loaded by legitimate services. Article-specific to the in-memory LionTail infection on critical Windows servers case study. Rationale: Check Point documents LionTail dropped to C:\Windows\System32 as wlanapi.dll or wlbsctrl.dll to exploit missing-DLL search-order hijacking on Windows Server. These phantom DLLs should never be written outside Windows servicing, so a non-servicing writer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2023/from-albania-to-the-middle-east-the-scarred-manticore-is-listening/ • https://www.securityweek.com/iranian-cyber-spies-use-liontail-malware-in-latest-attacks/
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1505.003 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windows servicing / cumulative update repopulating System32 via TiWorker/TrustedInstaller (excluded)
  • Third-party VPN/network driver installers that legitimately place wlanapi/wlbsctrl dependencies (verify signer)
  • Backup/restore agents rehydrating System32 during recovery
  • Image-deployment tooling (MDT/SCCM) writing a full System32 baseline
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped DLL and check signature/entropy; on servers, review which service loads it (RDP/WLAN services load wlbsctrl/TSVIPSrv) and inspect HTTP.sys usage. 2) Contain: isolate the server, capture memory (LionTail is memory-resident), and quarantine the DLL. 3) Hunt: pivot to WAF/network-tap logs for anomalous HTTP requests with attacker headers to IIS, and check other internet-facing Windows servers for the same phantom-DLL drop or named-pipe RCE.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\"
| where FileName in~ ("wlanapi.dll","wlbsctrl.dll","TSMSISrv.dll","TSVIPSrv.dll")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","wuauclt.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Windows\System32\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("wlanapi.dll","wlbsctrl.dll","TSMSISrv.dll","TSVIPSrv.dll")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("msiexec","TiWorker","TrustedInstaller","poqexec","wuauclt"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Dormant crypto-miner on servers: sustained stratum egress to mining pools AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts long-dormant cryptomining activity of the kind Kaspersky found running for four years on domain controllers: processes maintaining sustained outbound connections to public mining-pool ports / stratum endpoints. Article-specific to the missed-long-term crypto-mining-on-DC case study. Rationale: The case study is dormant crypto-mining persisting four years on domain controllers. Sustained (>5) outbound sessions from a single host/process to well-known stratum mining-pool ports, or to pool/xmr/monero URLs, is the network shape of a persistent miner and is highly abnormal on a DC. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/compromise-assessment-findings-2025/120542/
ATT&CKT1496 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate apps using high non-standard ports (some game servers, custom middleware on 7777/9999)
  • Blockchain/dev teams running sanctioned nodes or test miners
  • A monitoring agent probing infrastructure on overlapping ports
  • NAT/proxy egress consolidating many hosts' traffic onto shared destination ports
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","java.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess binary and path (miners hide in C:\Windows, ProgramData, or as a service); check CPU/GPU utilisation baseline and whether the host is a domain controller. 2) Contain: kill the process, block the pool IPs/ports at egress, and isolate the host — on a DC, treat as a full compromise and rotate krbtgt/privileged creds. 3) Hunt: baseline how long the process/service has existed (creation time), then sweep the estate for the same binary hash, service, and pool destinations to find co-infected hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where (RemotePort in (3333,4444,5555,7777,9999,14444,45560,45700)) or (RemoteUrl has_any ("xmr","monero","minexmr","supportxmr","nanopool","stratum","pool."))
| summarize ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where ConnCount > 5   // sustained, not a single stray connection
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3333,4444,5555,7777,9999,14444,45560,45700)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), DstIPs=make_set(DstIpAddr) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 5   // sustained mining beacon, not a one-off
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:3333 OR @DestinationPort:4444 OR @DestinationPort:5555 OR @DestinationPort:7777 OR @DestinationPort:9999 OR @DestinationPort:14444 OR @DestinationPort:45560 OR @DestinationPort:45700)

LoLBin abuse: certutil decode/urlcache, bitsadmin transfer, wmic process-call-create AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the living-off-the-land tooling Kaspersky says was present in every incident-yielding engagement: certutil.exe decoding/downloading payloads, bitsadmin.exe transferring files, and wmic.exe spawning processes. Article-specific to the 'Legitimate, yet suspicious: LoLBins and remote management tools' finding; deliberately excludes encoded-PowerShell (covered by existing rules). Rationale: Article states LoLBins/RMM tools appeared in every incident-yielding engagement. certutil -decode/-urlcache, bitsadmin /transfer, and wmic process-call-create are the specific abuse verbs (not raw execution), keeping FPs manageable while avoiding overlap with the existing encoded-PowerShell rule. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/compromise-assessment-findings-2025/120542/
ATT&CKT1140 T1105 T1047 T1197
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin scripts using certutil -urlcache to fetch installers or bitsadmin /transfer for patch staging
  • Legacy deployment tooling using wmic process call create for remote execution
  • Certificate lifecycle automation invoking certutil legitimately
  • Monitoring/inventory scripts that shell out to wmic
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","monitoringhost.exe","gpscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".corp",".local","patchmgmt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full command line — resolve the URL for certutil/bitsadmin and the target/command for wmic; check the parent process and whether the user is an admin/service account. 2) Contain: if the fetched file or wmic-created process is unknown, isolate the host and block the URL. 3) Hunt: pivot on the downloaded artifact hash and any child process it spawned across the estate; correlate with the same source IP/user performing remote wmic on multiple hosts (lateral movement).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "certutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-decode","/decode","-urlcache","/urlcache","-verifyctl"))
    or (FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/transfer")
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "process call create")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("-decode","/decode","-urlcache","/urlcache","-verifyctl"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "/transfer")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "process call create")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: LoLBin Abuse - certutil / bitsadmin / wmic Payload Handling
id: a7e14b39-5c62-49d8-b3a1-6f28de4c091b
description: Detects certutil decode/urlcache, bitsadmin transfer, and wmic process-call-create command lines associated with LoLBin-driven payload staging.
references:

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (((@Image:*\\certutil.exe OR @Image:*\\CertUtil.exe) AND (@CommandLine:*decode* OR @CommandLine:*urlcache* OR @CommandLine:*verifyctl*)) OR ((@Image:*\\bitsadmin.exe OR @Image:*\\BITSAdmin.exe) AND @CommandLine:*transfer*) OR ((@Image:*\\wmic.exe OR @Image:*\\WMIC.exe) AND @CommandLine:*process*call*create*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\certutil\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(-|\/)(decode|urlcache|verifyctl)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\bitsadmin\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\/transfer/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\wmic\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/process\s+call\s+create/i)
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])

Web shell execution: web server process spawning command interpreters AIExploitation High
Hunts web-shell-driven RCE where an IIS/Apache/Tomcat/PHP worker spawns a command interpreter or recon tool. Article-specific to the finding that 40% of discovered web shells lived in backups and were restored/reactivated; this catches the shell being used regardless of whether the file was flagged. Rationale: Article reports 40% of web shells hid in backups and reactivated. A web worker (w3wp/httpd/tomcat/php) spawning cmd/powershell/net/whoami/nltest is the execution signature of an active web shell and fires even when the shell file itself was never flagged. Distinct from the prohibited 'Office spawning scripts' rule. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/compromise-assessment-findings-2025/120542/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web apps that legitimately shell out (CI/CD agents, admin web consoles running diagnostics)
  • Monitoring plugins executing whoami/net for health checks under the app pool
  • Tomcat/Java apps invoking cmd for legitimate native integrations
  • Deployment scripts triggered via a web management interface
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\CI\\","apppool-diagnostics") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the web worker's recent request logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) around the timestamp to find the requesting IP and the shell URL/path. 2) Contain: pull the web-accessible directory offline or WAF-block the path, isolate the server, and preserve the web root + IIS logs. 3) Hunt: scan web roots (and restored-from-backup content) for *.asp/*.aspx/*.php/*.jsp files with recent write times or eval/exec patterns; sweep for the same client IP hitting other public apps.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe","tomcat.exe","java.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nltest.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\w3wp.exe","\\httpd.exe","\\nginx.exe","\\php-cgi.exe","\\php.exe","\\tomcat.exe","\\java.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\nltest.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Ghost x-ghost-preview cache-poisoning header in inbound HTTP requests (CVE-2026-53943)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated x-ghost-preview request to cached Ghost frontend (CVE-2026-53943 precondition) · [LLM] Ghost x-ghost-preview request carrying XSS payload markers (CVE-2026-53943 execution)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Ghost x-ghost-preview cache-poisoning header in inbound HTTP requests (CVE-2026-53943) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the internal-only x-ghost-preview request header arriving at a Ghost frontend that sits behind a shared cache (Fastly/Cloudflare/nginx proxy_cache). Presence of this header from external/unexpected sources is the precondition for CVE-2026-53943 cache-poisoning XSS, where a preview-altered response gets cached and served to other visitors. Rationale: Uses the exact header token 'x-ghost-preview' named in the advisory as the sole vulnerability trigger; this header is normally emitted only by Ghost's own admin preview flow, so its appearance in shared-cache proxy logs is inherently anomalous. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — HTTP request headers are not in EDR/CloudTrail schemas. Corroborated against GitLab Advisory DB and DailyCVE (CVSS 9.6). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/ghost/CVE-2026-53943/ • https://dailycve.com/ghost-cms-cache-poisoning-xss-cve-2026-53943-critical-dc-jul2026-821/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ghost editor/author using the built-in post-preview feature
  • Shared preview links opened by reviewers or marketing staff
  • CMS integration or headless-build job pre-rendering preview content
  • Synthetic monitoring / uptime checks configured to hit preview URLs
  • Internal QA automation validating draft rendering
Suppression filter
| where isempty(RequestCookies) or RequestCookies !has "ghost"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP(s) and confirm whether they belong to known editorial staff, CI/build systems, or monitoring. Check whether the same request also carried a valid Ghost session cookie (legit) or none (suspicious). 2) Contain: at the cache layer (Fastly/Cloudflare/nginx) add the documented workaround — bypass/vary cache for any request carrying x-ghost-preview — and confirm Ghost is upgraded to >=6.37.0. 3) Hunt: for each poisoned URL, check whether subsequent cache-HIT responses were served to other clients, and review admin/staff logons on the frontend domain for account takeover.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Message has "x-ghost-preview" or RequestContext has "x-ghost-preview"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 3f6c1e2a-9b4d-4c7e-8a11-2d5f7c9e4a10
status: experimental
description: Detects the internal-only x-ghost-preview request header at a Ghost frontend behind a shared cache, the precondition for CVE-2026-53943 cache-poisoning XSS.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-62q6-4hv4-vjrw
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/ghost/CVE-2026-53943/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  keywords:
    - 'x-ghost-preview'
  condition: keywords
level: medium
source:linux.syslog "x-ghost-preview"
CLOUD
index=web OR index=proxy (sourcetype="nginx:plus:access" OR sourcetype="nginx:access" OR sourcetype="access_combined" OR sourcetype="cloudflare:json" OR sourcetype="fastly") "x-ghost-preview"
| stats count as hits, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(uri_path) as uri_path, dc(clientip) as distinct_clients by host, sourcetype, clientip
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Unauthenticated x-ghost-preview request to cached Ghost frontend (CVE-2026-53943 precondition) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the x-ghost-preview header arrives with no session cookie present — the exact unauthenticated-attacker precondition the advisory calls out. Legitimate preview traffic carries a Ghost staff session; an anonymous request setting this header is an exploitation attempt against the shared cache. Rationale: Combines the advisory's exact header token with its stated precondition ('an unauthenticated user could send an x-ghost-preview header') by requiring absence of any Ghost session cookie, which cleanly separates malicious anonymous abuse from legit authenticated preview. Datadog/Sigma omitted — reliable cookie-absence negation is not expressible on free-text syslog or single-selection Sigma. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted (no HTTP header telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/ghost/CVE-2026-53943/ • https://dailycve.com/ghost-cms-cache-poisoning-xss-cve-2026-53943-critical-dc-jul2026-821/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or bug-bounty researcher probing the CVE
  • CDN misconfiguration that strips cookies before logging
  • Internal QA script deliberately exercising preview without login
  • Anonymized/privacy-proxy traffic that removes cookie headers before the WAF
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request had no valid Ghost staff session and identify the source IP/ASN and the targeted URL. A single anonymous host repeatedly setting x-ghost-preview across multiple URLs is high-confidence exploitation. 2) Contain: apply the cache-layer workaround (bypass cache on x-ghost-preview) immediately, block the offending source at the WAF, and confirm/schedule upgrade to Ghost >=6.37.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate every URL this source touched, check the cache for poisoned entries, and review staff-account activity on the frontend domain; if credential compromise is suspected use Ghost's 'Reset all authentication' (>=6.41.0).

| where Message has "x-ghost-preview" or RequestContext has "x-ghost-preview"
| where isempty(RequestCookies) or RequestCookies !has "ghost"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestCookies, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
