Ghost x-ghost-preview request carrying XSS payload markers (CVE-2026-53943 execution) AIExploitation High
Alerts when an x-ghost-preview request also contains HTML/JavaScript injection markers — the actual XSS payload that CVE-2026-53943 renders into the frontend response and stores in the shared cache to be served to subsequent visitors. Pairs the vulnerability trigger with the malicious content in one event. Rationale: Correlates the advisory's exact vulnerability trigger (x-ghost-preview) with classic reflected/stored XSS markers in the same request, capturing the injected content that gets rendered and cached ('served to subsequent visitors'). Very low FP because a preview request AND a script payload together has no benign explanation. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted — no HTTP payload telemetry in those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/ghost/CVE-2026-53943/ • https://dailycve.com/ghost-cms-cache-poisoning-xss-cve-2026-53943-critical-dc-jul2026-821/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated web vulnerability scanner (Burp/Acunetix/Nuclei) firing XSS probes with the preview header
  • Authorized penetration test validating CVE-2026-53943
  • WAF already blocked the request but still logged it (check DeviceAction/Activity)
  • Legitimate blog content whose title/body genuinely contains the literal string '<script' in a code sample
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "deny"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the injected payload from the request and the target URL; confirm whether the WAF blocked or passed it, and whether the response was subsequently cached and served (cache HIT) to other clients. 2) Contain: purge the affected URL(s) from the shared cache, apply the x-ghost-preview cache-bypass workaround, block the source IP, and verify Ghost is >=6.37.0. 3) Hunt: search staff logons on the frontend domain and any admin-session cookies for signs of takeover, review all URLs the source touched, and if compromise is confirmed invoke Ghost 'Reset all authentication' (>=6.41.0).

Fleet valuesFrom cross-namespace secret/configmap reference (CVE-2026-44935) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Rancher Fleet GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle custom resources whose spec contains a `valuesFrom` block with a secretKeyRef/configMapKeyRef, the exact mechanism CVE-2026-44935 abuses to read secrets in namespaces the tenant is not authorized for. Article-specific because it pivots on the Fleet CRD resource names plus the `valuesFrom` key-reference structure rather than generic secret access. Rationale: Uses the exact Fleet CRD resource names (gitrepos/helmops/bundles from go:github.com/rancher/fleet) and the `valuesFrom` + secretKeyRef/configMapKeyRef structure named in GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x as the exploitation vector; high-fidelity because legitimate fleet.yaml normally references secrets in the same namespace only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/007/
ATT&CKT1552.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-namespace GitOps deployment where an operator intentionally references a shared config namespace
  • Fleet platform team testing valuesFrom against a sanctioned central secrets namespace
  • CI pipelines that template Bundles with valuesFrom to a common values ConfigMap
  • Upgrade migrations that recreate existing GitRepo resources with unchanged valuesFrom blocks
Suppression filter
| where not (Username has "system:serviceaccount:cattle-fleet-system" and ObjNamespace == extract(@"namespace:\s*([a-z0-9-]+)", 1, ReqStr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestObject; compare the namespace inside valuesFrom to ObjectRef.namespace and to the tenant that owns the requesting Username — a mismatch to a namespace the tenant has no RBAC in is the true positive. 2) Contain: delete/suspend the offending GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle, and rotate any secret whose name/namespace/key appears in the valuesFrom reference (advisory explicitly recommends rotation). 3) Hunt: enumerate all Fleet CRs created by the same Username across the cluster and check whether the Fleet agent service account subsequently read those referenced secrets (see companion fan-out UC).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend ObjResource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), ObjNamespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where ObjResource in ("gitrepos","helmops","bundles")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has "valuesFrom" and (ReqStr has "secretKeyRef" or ReqStr has "configMapKeyRef")
| where ReqStr has "namespace"    // cross-namespace ref requires an explicit namespace inside valuesFrom
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, ObjResource, ObjNamespace, RequestUri, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fleet agent service account reads secrets across multiple namespaces (CVE-2026-44935) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream-cluster fingerprint of CVE-2026-44935: the Fleet agent service account issuing get/list of secrets or configmaps across an abnormal number of distinct namespaces within a short window, indicating cross-tenant credential harvesting via unrestricted valuesFrom/HelmOp deployment. Article-specific because it keys on the Fleet agent SA identity and the cross-namespace fan-out the advisory tells defenders to review logs for. Rationale: Pivots on the Fleet agent service account identity (cattle-fleet-system fleet-agent) reading secrets/configmaps across namespaces — the exact post-exploit behaviour GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x tells operators to review cluster logs for and to drive credential rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/007/
ATT&CKT1552.007 T1613
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-tenant cluster where the Fleet agent SA is authorized to deploy into many namespaces by design
  • Initial Fleet onboarding/bootstrap that syncs bundles into a large set of namespaces at once
  • Backup/DR tooling running under a fleet-labelled SA enumerating secrets
  • Cluster-wide chart rollout (e.g. cert-manager, monitoring) driven through Fleet touching every namespace
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct namespaces and secret names the Fleet agent SA touched; confirm against the tenant boundary — reads into namespaces owned by a different tenant are the true positive. 2) Contain: rotate the Fleet agent service account token and every secret it read cross-tenant, then apply the patched-version Policy resource pinning a least-privilege service account per GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle namespace. 3) Hunt: correlate back to companion UC (valuesFrom cross-namespace references) to identify which GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle CR triggered the reads and which tenant Username authored it; upgrade Fleet to v0.15.2/v0.14.6/0.13.11/v0.12.15.

Rancher /v3/import authImage YAML injection via URL-encoded newlines (CVE-2026-44939) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound web requests to the Rancher cluster-import endpoint /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml where the authImage query parameter carries URL-encoded newlines (%0A/%0D) or raw newlines — the exact YAML-breakout primitive used to inject arbitrary manifest keys. Article-specific because it keys on the concrete endpoint path plus the authImage parameter plus the newline breakout characters, not a generic web attack. Rationale: Uses the exact article strings: endpoint '/v3/import/', parameter 'authImage', and the URL-encoded newline breakout (%0A/%0D) named as the patch target. Legitimate agent-image overrides never contain newline encodings, so FP rate is very low. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44939 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rancher/rancher/CVE-2026-44939/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1190 T1610
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing the /v3/import endpoint with crafted payloads during authorized pentests
  • Rancher agent troubleshooting where an operator manually URL-encodes an image tag containing a '+' or ':' (rare, and won't include %0A/%0D)
  • WAF/proxy that double-decodes and re-logs the query string, producing a benign echoed value
  • Automated CI that templates import URLs and accidentally embeds a trailing whitespace character
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","nuclei","Nuclei","masscan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL and URL-decode the authImage value; confirm it contains newline bytes followed by injected YAML keys (command:, hostPath, hostNetwork). Note SourceIP and whether the request returned 200. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, invalidate/rotate the affected cluster registration token, and confirm Rancher is on a patched build (>= 2.14.2/2.13.6/2.12.10/2.11.14/2.10.12). 3) Hunt: pivot to Kubernetes audit logs for any DaemonSet create/update in cattle-system named kube-api-auth carrying command:/args:, and search endpoints for kubectl apply of the same import URL.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/v3/import/"
| where RequestURL has "authImage"
| where RequestURL has_any ("%0A","%0a","%0D","%0d","%0d%0a","\n","\r")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ReceivedBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rancher authImage YAML Injection via Encoded Newline (CVE-2026-44939)
id: 5f2b7e40-3c9a-4d21-9b6e-7a1c2f8e44d1
description: Detects requests to the Rancher /v3/import cluster-import endpoint where the authImage query parameter contains URL-encoded or raw newlines used to break out of the YAML image field.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44939
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1610
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-query|contains|all:
      - 'authImage'
    c-uri|contains: '/v3/import/'
  newline:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - '%0A'
      - '%0a'
      - '%0D'
      - '%0d'
  condition: selection and newline
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v3/import/*" Web.url="*authImage*" (Web.url="*%0A*" OR Web.url="*%0a*" OR Web.url="*%0D*" OR Web.url="*%0d*" OR Web.url="*%0d%0a*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v3/import/*" Web.url="*authImage*" (Web.url="*%0A*" OR Web.url="*%0a*" OR Web.url="*%0D*" OR Web.url="*%0d*" OR Web.url="*%0d%0a*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
kubectl apply of attacker-crafted Rancher import URL (authImage payload delivery) AIDelivery High
Detects a cluster operator fetching or applying the malicious Rancher import manifest — kubectl/oc apply or curl/wget against a URL containing /v3/import/ and the authImage parameter. This is the victim-side delivery step the advisory requires ('victim must execute kubectl apply against a maliciously crafted URL'). Rationale: Anchors on the article's required victim action (kubectl apply of a crafted URL) plus the concrete '/v3/import/' path and 'authImage' parameter, matched in the process command line — near-zero legitimate use of that exact combination. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62 • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security engineer reproducing/validating the CVE in a lab against a patched Rancher instance
  • Legitimate Rancher onboarding where an operator applies a genuine import URL (will NOT contain a newline-laden authImage, but the URL path matches) — inspect the decoded authImage value
  • Documentation or runbook automation that curls the import manifest for archival
  • Vulnerability scanners that shell out to curl against the import endpoint
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("%0A","%0a","%0D","%0d") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"authImage=[^\s&]*(command|hostPath|hostNetwork)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: URL-decode the authImage value in the captured command line; benign onboarding has an OCI image reference, exploitation has embedded newlines + injected YAML keys. Identify the operator account and host. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the manifest was applied, revoke the cluster registration token used in the URL, and rotate the cattle service account and any cluster credentials per the advisory guidance. 3) Hunt: query Kubernetes audit logs for the resulting DaemonSet in cattle-system and check control-plane nodes for containers spawned from the injected command: field.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("kubectl","kubectl.exe","oc","oc.exe","curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/v3/import/"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "authImage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("kubectl","oc","curl","wget")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/v3/import/"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "authImage"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rancher /v3/import registration-token enumeration or cross-source reuse AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts abuse of the cluster-import endpoint: a single source IP requesting many distinct registration tokens (enumeration) — the /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml format is token-gated and the advisory notes tokens leak via docs/screenshots. Surfaces reconnaissance and leaked-token reuse ahead of the actual injection. Rationale: Derives the token position directly from the article's endpoint format /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml and the advisory's note that these tokens leak; counting distinct tokens per source IP is the cleanest enumeration signal available in web logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1190 T1589
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Rancher management/monitoring host polling many downstream cluster import URLs legitimately (allowlist its IP)
  • Load balancer or NAT egress IP aggregating many legitimate operators behind one source address
  • CI/CD automation that bulk-registers clusters during a fleet rollout
  • Backup/inventory tooling walking the Rancher API
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 rancher-mgmt-nat")  // replace with your Rancher management egress IPs after baseline
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the SourceIP's request pattern — is it a known Rancher management node/NAT, or an unfamiliar external IP hitting many tokens in seconds? Check whether any request also carried an authImage newline payload. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, block the SourceIP and invalidate all registration tokens it touched; rotate tokens that may have leaked via docs/screenshots. 3) Hunt: for each token the source successfully retrieved, look for a follow-on kubectl apply on operator endpoints and for new DaemonSets in cattle-system on the corresponding downstream clusters.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "/v3/import/"
| extend Token = extract(@"/v3/import/([A-Za-z0-9]+)_", 1, RequestURL)
| where isnotempty(Token)
| summarize DistinctTokens = dcount(Token), SampleTokens = make_set(Token, 15), Requests = count(), DestHosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 5) by SourceIP
| where DistinctTokens >= 5   // 5+ distinct registration tokens from one source in 24h = token enumeration
| order by DistinctTokens desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v3/import/*" by Web.src, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rex field=url "/v3/import/(?<token>[A-Za-z0-9]+)_"
| where isnotnull(token)
| stats dc(token) as distinct_tokens values(token) as tokens sum(count) as requests by src
| where distinct_tokens >= 5
| sort - distinct_tokens
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v3/import/*" by Web.src, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rex field=url "/v3/import/(?<token>[A-Za-z0-9]+)_"
| where isnotnull(token)

| where distinct_tokens >= 5
| sort - distinct_tokens

easy-day-js second-stage C2 beacon to Mastra supply-chain infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the hardcoded C2 IPs and domains used by the second-stage payload dropped by the malicious easy-day-js typosquat during the June 2026 Mastra npm compromise. Any host reaching 23.254.164.92/.123, teams.onweblive.org or maskasd.com is a confirmed post-install callback. Rationale: Uses the five article-supplied network IOCs (23.254.164.92, 23.254.164.123, teams.onweblive.org, maskasd.com) that are the dropper's second-stage callback destinations — exact-match on attacker infra is inherently high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domains
  • Recycled hosting IP later reassigned to a benign tenant on 23.254.164.0/24
  • Proxy/egress appliance logging the block as an allowed-then-denied event
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") // exclude analyst manual IOC lookups in a browser
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if node.exe/npm confirms a compromised dependency install; pull the host's package tree and the Secure Registry Policy Evaluations log for that device. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 23.254.164.92/.123 and the two domains at egress, revoke any credentials/tokens present on the machine or CI runner. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and for node_modules/easy-day-js, and for any host that pulled a Mastra-ecosystem package in the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123") or RemoteUrl in~ ("teams.onweblive.org", "maskasd.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123") or DstHostname in~ ("teams.onweblive.org", "maskasd.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node postinstall script spawning a download or shell process (Mastra dropper pattern) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the obfuscated postinstall dropper behaviour from the easy-day-js compromise: the npm/node package-manager process spawning powershell/curl/certutil/cmd to pull a second-stage payload immediately after install. Targets the parent→child chain rooted in node_modules. Rationale: Grounds on the article's described TTP — an obfuscated postinstall dropper that fetches a second-stage from an attacker server — expressed as the node/npm parent spawning a download/shell child in node_modules context. Behavioural, not IOC-bound, so it catches future variants.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native-module packages (node-gyp) shelling out to cmd/python during install
  • Dev tooling that runs curl in a postinstall to fetch platform binaries (e.g. puppeteer, esbuild)
  • CI runners executing lifecycle scripts that legitimately call PowerShell
  • Corporate npm packages with signed postinstall bootstrap scripts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","puppeteer") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("iex","-enc","FromBase64String"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line — a URL to a non-registry host or base64/obfuscated PowerShell confirms malice; cross-reference the device against Secure Registry to see which package version was installed. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, block the fetched URL, snapshot node_modules before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved second-stage URL and on the C2 IOCs (23.254.164.92/.123), and enumerate every host that installed a Mastra-ecosystem package.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "npm.exe", "npm.cmd")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "cscript.exe", "wscript.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "bash.exe", "wget.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node_modules" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "postinstall" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe", "npm.exe", "npm.cmd")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "cscript.exe", "wscript.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "node_modules" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "postinstall" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious easy-day-js typosquat package written into node_modules AIDelivery High
Detects the presence of the easy-day-js typosquat (of dayjs) being dropped into a node_modules directory on developer machines or CI runners — the initial-access artifact of the June 2026 Mastra npm supply-chain compromise. Any host with this path pulled the compromised dependency. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package name (easy-day-js) named in the article as the typosquat added across 140+ Mastra packages — a filesystem path containing that string is an unambiguous indicator of the compromised dependency.
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally staging the sample for analysis in a lab node_modules
  • A benign future package legitimately named similarly (low likelihood — name is the malicious artifact)
  • SCA/dependency-scanning tooling caching the package name in a report file on disk
  • Git repo containing a historical lockfile reference cloned to disk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact version installed and whether the postinstall dropper ran (check for child processes of node/npm and the C2 IOCs); use Secure Registry to enumerate every machine/pipeline that pulled it. 2) Contain: isolate affected hosts, purge node_modules, remove easy-day-js from lockfiles, rotate any secrets exposed on those machines/runners. 3) Hunt: expand to all Mastra-ecosystem packages and to the sibling GitHub Actions compromises (codfish/semantic-release-action, simonecorsi/mawesome) in CI logs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "easy-day-js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "easy-day-js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Package-manager dropper self-deletion inside node_modules (evidence erasure) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the anti-forensic self-deletion described in the Mastra compromise: after fetching the second stage, the postinstall dropper deletes itself to erase evidence. Flags node/npm deleting script files it just wrote under node_modules. Rationale: Grounds on the article's explicit anti-forensic claim that the dropper 'deleted itself to erase the evidence' — expressed as node/npm deleting script files under node_modules, a rare and suspicious combination distinct from normal install churn.
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm ci / clean-install wiping and rebuilding node_modules
  • Package upgrade removing an old dependency version's files
  • Yarn/pnpm cache pruning invoked via node
  • Build tooling that deletes generated .js artifacts under node_modules during a rebuild
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ci","clean-install","rimraf","prune")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the deletion with a preceding FileWritten of the same file and any node→shell/download spawn within seconds; check the device in Secure Registry for a recently pulled package. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the disk/memory image before further churn, block the C2 IOCs. 3) Hunt: recover the deleted file from backups/VSS for analysis, and sweep the fleet for the same delete pattern plus easy-day-js and the C2 destinations.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".cjs" or FileName endswith ".sh"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileDeleted"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe", "npm.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js" or TargetFileName endswith ".cjs" or TargetFileName endswith ".sh"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known-malicious Mastra supply-chain payload file hashes on disk or in execution AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on the specific SHA256/SHA1 payload hashes tied to the easy-day-js dropper and its second stage from the Mastra npm compromise. Matches whether the artifact is written to disk or executed, giving a direct confirmation pivot for scoped hosts. Rationale: Uses the five SHA256 and one SHA1 hash IOCs supplied with the article — direct file-hash matches on the dropper/second-stage payloads are the highest-fidelity confirmation available for scoped hosts.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst holding a sample copy on an EDR-monitored analysis host
  • Backup/quarantine system retaining a copy of the flagged file
  • Threat-intel feed distributing the sample to a detonation VM
  • Hash collision (cryptographically implausible — effectively none)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path and initiating process; a match under node_modules or executed by node/npm confirms the supply-chain vector — enumerate the device in Secure Registry. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, quarantine the file, block the C2 IOCs, and rotate exposed credentials/tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 IPs/domains and on easy-day-js across the fleet, and validate whether any second-stage persistence or lateral movement followed.
union DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
    or SHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access

            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:

            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents

// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine

union

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

Multiple @immobiliarelabs Backstage Plugins Compromised on npm

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 12 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Compromised versions run a malicious payload at npm install time through a binding.gyp node-gyp hook, harvesting credentials from sources like GitHub Actions secrets, cloud provider keys, and package registry tokens, while trying to persist in AI coding assistant configs. Static analysis of version 2.1.2 against the clean 2.1.1 release revealed a new 5 MB index.js and an added binding.gyp, both absent from earlier releases.

Phantom Gyp binding.gyp install-time payload execution (Miasma npm worm) AIInstallation High
Hunts the GYP command-expansion shell invocation that the Miasma/Phantom Gyp worm plants in binding.gyp to run the 5 MB index.js during node-gyp configure, bypassing scripts.postinstall monitoring. The exact source line is '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)', so a process command line carrying both 'node index.js' and 'echo stub.c' is the worm firing. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim binding.gyp source string '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)' from the article; the 'node index.js' + 'echo stub.c' pairing is unique to the Phantom Gyp configure-step trick and not a legitimate gyp pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native addon packages whose binding.gyp uses node-based command expansion (rare; almost never invokes a bare index.js with echo stub.c)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • CI job intentionally re-running the malicious tarball for analysis
  • A developer's own gyp build script that happens to echo a stub source file
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain (npm/node-gyp/sh) and identify which @immobiliarelabs (or other) package was being installed; confirm a 5 MB index.js + binding.gyp exist in that package dir. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, revoke any tokens that were live in that session (GitHub, npm, cloud), and rotate CI secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: search the same host for a Bun binary in temp, IMDS (169.254.169.254) hits, and writes to AI-assistant configs (.claude/settings.json etc.); pivot org-wide on the affected package@version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime executing a temp payload spawned by node (Miasma Node.js-monitoring evasion) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the deliberate runtime switch where the Miasma loader downloads Bun (bun-v1.3.13) and runs the decrypted credential-harvester from a randomly named temp file under Bun instead of Node, to evade --require-hook security tooling. A bun process whose parent is node/npm/node-gyp/sh and that executes a file from /tmp or /var/folders is the second stage. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit detail that the loader downloads Bun (bun-v1.3.13) and executes the decrypted main payload from a randomly named temp file under Bun specifically to dodge Node's --require interception; node-parent + bun-child + temp path is the distinguishing shape. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-malware-uses-binding-gyp-and-bun/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1027 T1059.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers who legitimately use Bun as their runtime/test-runner invoked from npm scripts
  • Bun-based build tooling executing cached transpiled output from a temp dir
  • Monorepo task runners (turbo/nx) shelling out to bun for a subpackage
  • CI images that prewarm Bun and run scratch scripts from /tmp
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the temp file path bun executed and hash it; check whether the project legitimately depends on Bun (package.json/engines) — a Bun execution with no Bun dependency declared is high-signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the bun process tree, and quarantine the temp payload before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: correlate to a binding.gyp install in the prior 5 minutes, then look for IMDS/metadata access and AI-assistant config writes from the same session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun" or FileName startswith "bun-"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp","yarn","pnpm")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/","/var/tmp/") or FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/","/var/tmp/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime Executing Temp Payload Spawned by Node (Miasma Evasion)

description: Detects the Miasma loader's runtime switch where a Bun process spawned by node/npm/node-gyp runs a decrypted payload from a temp directory to evade Node.js --require security hooks.

Miasma infectHost persistence in AI coding assistant configs AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the infectHost routine that backdoors AI coding-assistant configuration files for re-execution: .claude/settings.json (SessionStart hook), .vscode/tasks.json (folderOpen), .cursor/rules/, .aider.conf.yml, and .github/copilot-instructions.md. Filters to writes performed by node/bun/npm so legit editor saves are excluded. Rationale: Directly maps the article's infectHost target list (Claude Code SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json, VS Code folderOpen in .vscode/tasks.json, .cursor/rules, .aider.conf.yml, .github/copilot-instructions.md); requiring a node/bun writer separates the malware from legitimate IDE saves. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1546 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's VS Code / Cursor extension (which runs under node) legitimately writing tasks.json or rules on project open
  • Aider itself updating .aider.conf.yml during normal use
  • Dotfile-management tooling (chezmoi/yadm) restoring AI-assistant configs
  • An MCP/agent framework legitimately writing a SessionStart hook into .claude/settings.json
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code","cursor","aider") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code","cursor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written config and inspect the hook/command body — Miasma injects a shell/JS command into the SessionStart, folderOpen, or rules entry; benign saves contain no execution directive. 2) Contain: revert the config from version control, remove the injected hook, and isolate the host if a command was present. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/home dir on the host for the same five config files, and check whether the SessionStart hook already fired (child processes of the AI assistant).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.claude/settings.json", "/.vscode/tasks.json", "/.cursor/rules", "/.aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md") or FileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where FolderPath has_any (".claude",".vscode",".cursor",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (".claude/settings.json", ".vscode/tasks.json", ".cursor/rules", ".aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud instance-metadata harvesting from npm/node install context (Miasma credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Miasma harvester reaching AWS IMDS (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-metadata (169.254.170.2) from a node/bun/npm/node-gyp process — the exact endpoints the article lists for cloud credential theft. Scoped to install-tooling parents and the Bun stage so it isn't a long-running app's normal SDK traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's literal credential-source endpoints (IMDS 169.254.169.254 and ECS metadata 169.254.170.2) tied to the npm/node/Bun execution context; metadata access from package-install tooling (vs a steady-state app) is the high-fidelity differentiator. Sentinel left empty because ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process attribution to bind the IMDS hit to node/bun. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js app on EC2/ECS legitimately using the AWS SDK to refresh instance-role credentials via IMDS
  • CI tooling (e.g. node-based deploy scripts) that queries instance identity at job start
  • Container health agents written in node polling task metadata
  • Infra-as-code node CLIs (CDK) resolving region/account from IMDS
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "aws-sdk" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("systemd","pm2","forever")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the calling process lineage — IMDS access from a process whose parent is npm/node-gyp/sh during a package install, or from a Bun temp process, is not normal SDK usage. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate the instance-role / task-role credentials and any cloud keys reachable from that role; review CloudTrail for use of those creds from new IPs. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on reads of /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem, Vault token files (/home/runner/.vault-token, /root/.vault-token, /run/secrets/VAULT_TOKEN), and .ssh/ on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","dash","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","dash","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

Compromised @immobiliarelabs Backstage plugin on disk (binding.gyp + index.js / known hashes) AIDelivery Medium
Inventory/IOC detection for the trojanized @immobiliarelabs/backstage-plugin-gitlab(-backend) and backstage-plugin-ldap-auth(-backend) packages. Clean releases never shipped a binding.gyp, so the presence of binding.gyp or the 5 MB index.js inside those package paths — or any file matching the three published malicious SHA256s — confirms a compromised version was installed. Rationale: Built on the article's affected-package matrix plus the three published SHA256 IOCs; a binding.gyp inside these specific Backstage plugin directories is itself anomalous because the clean 2.1.1-era releases shipped neither binding.gyp nor a 5 MB index.js. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-6527 • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally staging the malicious tarball in an isolated analysis sandbox
  • A cached npm tarball retained on a build agent after remediation (already-known, low risk)
  • An offline mirror/proxy (Verdaccio/Artifactory) holding a quarantined copy for inspection
  • Hash collision is implausible — SHA256 matches are definitive
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact package@version from the path against the affected matrix (gitlab/gitlab-backend 3.0.3–7.0.2, 1.0.1, 2.1.2; ldap-auth(-backend) 1.1.3/1.1.4–5.2.1) and check whether node-gyp executed it (install actually ran). 2) Contain: pin/roll back to a known-clean version, purge the tarball from caches and lockfiles, isolate affected build agents, and rotate every credential reachable from that host/CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to binding.gyp execution, Bun temp execution, IMDS access, and AI-assistant config writes on the same hosts; sweep the registry/repo org for republished (worm-propagated) packages from any maintainer account touched by these runners.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and FileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (TargetFilePath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or TargetFilePath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and TargetFileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Jackson Maven typosquat C2 — beacon to fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82 AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the namespace-impersonation C2 (fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org) or the staging IP 103.127.243.82 used by the malicious org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind artifact to pull a Cobalt Strike beacon. Article-specific: these are typosquats of the legitimate fasterxml.com / com.fasterxml namespace, so any hit is high-fidelity. Rationale: fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org and 103.127.243.82:8000 are the verbatim C2 from Aikido's analysis (config.txt + svchosts.exe staging), typosquatting the real fasterxml.com — so any resolution/connection is malicious by definition. Cross-checked Aikido and cybersecuritynews/SC Media. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-infiltrated-maven-central/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/maven-central-subjected-to-typosquatted-jackson-json-library
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or researcher detonating the sample in-house
  • Threat-intel proxy / URL-crawler pre-resolving the IOC domain
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ responding to the domain (benign, but worth confirming sink not real resolve)
  • Internal artifact-mirror health-check probing the coordinate's declared SCM/URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") // exclude analyst browser lookups of the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess (expect java.exe/javaw.exe from a Spring Boot app or CI runner); confirm whether the resolve led to an actual TCP connect to 103.127.243.82:8000 or :51211. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82 at egress, and pull the build's dependency tree for org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind. 3) Hunt: sweep all CI runners and dev machines that resolved org.fasterxml namespace coordinates, and pivot to UC2/UC3 for dropped svchosts.exe / payload.bin and the two SHA256 implants.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has "fasterxml.org" or RemoteIP == "103.127.243.82"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Java/Spring drops & runs svchosts.exe (svchost masquerade) — Jackson typosquat implant AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage drop where the malicious JacksonSpringAutoConfiguration class writes payload.bin to temp and executes svchosts.exe (a typosquat of the legitimate svchost.exe). Article-specific via the exact filenames and the java.exe→svchosts.exe parent/child chain. Rationale: svchosts.exe (note trailing 's') is never a legitimate Windows binary and is the verbatim Windows payload name; pairing the java.exe parent with the two confirmed SHA256 implants makes this near-zero-FP. Sourced from Aikido's payload breakdown. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-infiltrated-maven-central/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or pentester naming an unrelated test binary svchosts.exe
  • Red-team tooling intentionally masquerading as svchost
  • Unrelated commodity malware reusing the svchosts.exe name (still malicious — escalate)
  • EDR sample-replay / detonation lab running the captured artifact
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Tests\", @"\redteam\")) // suppress sanctioned test/red-team binaries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary path (expect a temp/working dir, not System32) and parent (java.exe/javaw.exe from a Spring Boot app or CI build); validate SHA256 against the two known implant hashes. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, and quarantine svchosts.exe / payload.bin; block the C2 from UC1. 3) Hunt: search the host and peers for the hidden .idea.pid persistence marker, for beacons to 103.127.243.82:8000 / m.fasterxml.org:51211, and audit which builds resolved org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchosts.exe"
   or SHA256 in ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f","702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "svchosts.exe"
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe") and TargetProcessName has "svchosts.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Jackson typosquat Cobalt Strike implant hash sighting (Win + macOS/Linux) AIInstallation Medium
Vector-agnostic sweep for the two confirmed implant SHA256 hashes (svchosts.exe for Windows, 'update' for macOS/Linux) dropped by the malicious jackson-databind artifact. Catches the implant even when delivered outside the java→svchosts.exe chain (e.g. pulled directly into a CI cache). Rationale: The two SHA256 are the verbatim VirusTotal-confirmed Cobalt Strike beacons (Windows svchosts.exe + macOS/Linux 'update') from Aikido's IOC list; an exact-hash match is effectively zero-FP and covers non-Windows hosts the process/network UCs miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://www.scworld.com/brief/maven-central-subjected-to-typosquatted-jackson-json-library

  • Backup/forensic image containing a previously quarantined copy
  • Sandbox detonation lab re-fetching the sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe") // exclude AV/EDR quarantine writes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process and path — distinguish an AV/EDR quarantine vault (benign) from a live drop in a build/temp dir (true positive). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, and revoke any CI/cloud credentials reachable from the build that pulled jackson-databind (Cobalt Strike harvests CI secrets). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (C2 to fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82) and UC2 (svchosts.exe execution) on the same and neighbouring hosts, and inventory every repo/runner that resolved org.fasterxml.jackson.core coordinates.

| where SHA256 in ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f","702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or SHA1 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or MD5 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or SHA1 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd") or MD5 in~ ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f", "702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker published malicious versions of 20 npm packages belonging to the Leo Platform ecosystem in a coordinated burst spanning less than three seconds. All 20 packages carry an identical CI/CD attack toolkit that steals secrets from GitHub Actions runners, cloud credential stores, package registries, and password managers, then exfiltrates them via the victim's own GitHub token. Together these packages receive approximately 13,600 downloads per week.

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Bun executes dropped temp payload /tmp/p*.js (Miasma stealer launch) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Passwordless sudo backdoor written for runner account (runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun v1.3.13 runtime pulled from GitHub Releases during npm install (Phantom Gyp staging)
