ScreenConnect service drops and executes VBS/PS loader files in C:\Users\Public AIExploitation High
Hunts the loader stage: the ScreenConnect service creates script.vbs, cap.ps1, secret_bytes.txt, msgbox.txt and 1.vb in C:\Users\Public and launches script.vbs/cap.ps1 (hidden window). script.vbs also kills all powershell.exe to cover tracks. Article-specific via the exact filenames and the ScreenConnect→wscript/powershell parent chain out of the Public directory. Rationale: The loader filenames (script.vbs, cap.ps1, secret_bytes.txt, installer_method3_stream.vbs) written to C:\Users\Public by a ScreenConnect/wscript parent are exact article IOCs; the Public-directory staging plus reflective-load chain is distinct from generic 'script in temp' noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.esentire.com/blog/exploring-the-infection-chain-screenconnects-link-to-asyncrat-deployment • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/trojanized-screenconnect-installers-evolve-dropping-multiple-rats-on-a-single-machine/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.001 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business app legitimately staging scripts in C:\Users\Public
  • Admin logon/startup script writing helper VBS to the Public profile
  • Software installer using Public as a shared working directory
  • Security tooling writing named files that coincidentally overlap (rare given exact names)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process is ScreenConnect/wscript and inspect secret_bytes.txt for the [SXX- encoded PE pattern; check whether cap.ps1 ran hidden and whether powershell.exe was mass-killed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill wscript/RegAsm, delete the C:\Users\Public loader set, and remove the ScreenConnect service. 3) HUNT: Pivot to RegAsm.exe process hollowing / C2 to mora1987[.]work[.]gd and the MasterPackager.Updater scheduled task; sweep the fleet for the same Public-directory files.
let loaderFiles = dynamic(["script.vbs","cap.ps1","secret_bytes.txt","msgbox.txt","1.vb","installer_method3_stream.vbs"]);
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\Users\Public" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("script.vbs","cap.ps1","secret_bytes.txt","installer_method3_stream.vbs")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath startswith @"C:\Users\Public" and FileName in~ (loaderFiles)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl","wscript.exe")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath )
| order by Timestamp desc
let loaderFiles = dynamic(["script.vbs","cap.ps1","secret_bytes.txt","msgbox.txt","1.vb","installer_method3_stream.vbs"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "C:\\Users\\Public" and TargetFileName in~ (loaderFiles)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task MasterPackager.Updater re-launching wscript C:\Users\Public\script.vbs every 2 minutes AIInstallation High
Hunts the campaign's persistence: a schtasks-created task named MasterPackager.Updater running wscript.exe against C:\Users\Public\script.vbs on a 2-minute recurrence (/SC MINUTE /MO 2). Article-specific via the exact task name, target script path, and aggressive recurrence. Rationale: Task name MasterPackager.Updater plus the wscript C:\Users\Public\script.vbs target and /SC MINUTE /MO 2 recurrence are verbatim from the article — the exact task name makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.esentire.com/blog/exploring-the-infection-chain-screenconnects-link-to-asyncrat-deployment
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app named 'MasterPackager' installing its own updater task (verify signed publisher path)
  • Admin creating a frequent maintenance task pointing at a Public-profile script
  • RMM tooling creating minute-cadence tasks for monitoring
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the task action — a 2-minute wscript task against C:\Users\Public\script.vbs is malicious regardless of the friendly name; confirm the creating user/process. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the task (schtasks /Delete /TN MasterPackager.Updater /F), isolate the host, remove the referenced loader files. 3) HUNT: Sweep the fleet for the MasterPackager.Updater task and for RegAsm.exe beaconing to mora1987[.]work[.]gd; check for the ScreenConnect service and Defender exclusions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "MasterPackager.Updater"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "/Create" and ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\Users\Public\script.vbs" and ProcessCommandLine has "wscript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698   // A scheduled task was created
| where EventData has "MasterPackager.Updater" or (EventData has "script.vbs" and EventData has "Users\\Public")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RegAsm.exe (hollowed) beaconing to AsyncRAT C2 / ScreenConnect infra contacts campaign IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 stage: RegAsm.exe — a .NET utility that should never make external network connections — reaching out to the AsyncRAT C2 domain mora1987[.]work[.]gd after process hollowing, plus ScreenConnect/loader processes contacting the campaign's fixed C2 IPs (162.216.241[.]242, 198.23.185[.]81, 2.59.134[.]97) and domains (r.servermanagemen[.]xyz). Article-specific via the concrete C2 indicators and the anomalous RegAsm egress. Rationale: mora1987[.]work[.]gd, r.servermanagemen[.]xyz and the three C2 IPs are article IOCs corroborated by Kaspersky's infrastructure clustering; RegAsm.exe making any public connection is inherently anomalous (it never networks legitimately) and is the AsyncRAT process-hollowing container from the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.esentire.com/blog/exploring-the-infection-chain-screenconnects-link-to-asyncrat-deployment • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A rare .NET dev/build scenario where RegAsm.exe is scripted to reach a package feed (uncommon; verify path and parent)
  • Shared C2 IP later reassigned to a benign hoster (validate against current threat-intel)
  • Proxy/NAT egress attributing the connection to an unexpected source host
  • Internal vuln scanner probing the campaign IPs during authorized testing
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RegAsm.exe" and RemoteUrl has_any ("nuget.org","microsoft.com") and RemoteIP !in (c2ip))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm RegAsm.exe was spawned suspended by the loader chain (parent = script/cap.ps1 lineage) and correlate the C2 destination against threat-intel; RegAsm networking is by itself high-confidence malicious. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill RegAsm.exe, block the C2 IPs/domains at perimeter, and remove the ScreenConnect service + persistence task. 3) HUNT: Sweep DeviceNetworkEvents fleet-wide for the C2 IPs/domains and for any RegAsm.exe/AppLaunch.exe public egress; correlate to hosts with the C:\Users\Public loader set.
let c2ip = dynamic(["162.216.241.242","198.23.185.81","2.59.134.97"]);
let c2dom = dynamic(["mora1987.work.gd","r.servermanagemen.xyz"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ip)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (c2dom)
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RegAsm.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ip = dynamic(["162.216.241.242","198.23.185.81","2.59.134.97"]);
let c2dom = dynamic(["mora1987.work.gd","r.servermanagemen.xyz"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (c2ip) or DstHostname has_any (c2dom) or Url has_any (c2dom)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or SHA1 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or MD5 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or SHA1 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or MD5 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["87603ea025623b19954e460add532048"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken: Inside an EvilTokens affiliate panel targeting Microsoft 365

Cisco Talos
2026-07-01 16 use cases 12 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Talos has identified "ARToken," a phishing-as-a-service platform that targets Microsoft 365. The ARToken panel exposes 80+ API endpoints for device code phishing, Primary Refresh Token persistence, email access, BEC operations, and SharePoint exfiltration.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint egress to ARToken C2 / phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com, workers.dev) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

ARToken vendor-impersonation phish: inbound mail failing SPF+DKIM+DMARC with pumber.png signature lure AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ARToken initial-access email that spoofs a trusted vendor's accounts-payable contact: inbound, delivered, all three sender-auth checks (SPF, DKIM body-hash, DMARC compauth=none) failing, carrying the outstanding-invoice lure. Anchored on the article's inline signature attachment pumber.png to raise fidelity above generic auth-fail noise. Rationale: Combines the article's stated triple auth-failure (compauth=none reason=405) with the concrete inline signature attachment pumber.png and the outstanding-invoice lure theme — far higher fidelity than auth-fail alone. Reply-To vs From pivot noted by Talos is not a first-class column in the mail-security schemas, so pumber.png + full auth failure is the durable anchor.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor whose mail server misconfigures SPF/DKIM and coincidentally attaches an image named pumber.png (extremely unlikely)
  • Marketing/newsletter senders from mis-delegated subdomains failing all three checks
  • Forwarded internal mail losing DKIM alignment
  • A genuine AP invoice thread where the vendor's DMARC broke after a DNS change
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("yourtrusteddomain.com") // maintain an allowlist of vendor domains that legitimately fail alignment post-DNS-change
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the message, confirm SenderFromAddress domain is a known vendor while SenderMailFromAddress/sending IP is unrelated, and check the Reply-To header for an off-domain redirect. 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete via EmailPostDeliveryEvents, block the Reply-To domain, and warn the recipient AP mailbox. 3) Hunt: search for other recipients of the same pumber.png attachment or the same sending IP, and pivot any embedded *.sharepoint.com anchor into UC 'SharePoint tenant lookalike'.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| extend AD = parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)
| where tostring(AD.SPF) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DKIM) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DMARC) =~ "fail"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "pumber.png"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SigImage = FileName
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SigImage, SenderIPv4, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| extend AD = parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)
| where tostring(AD.SPF) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DKIM) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DMARC) =~ "fail"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "pumber.png"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SigImage = FileName
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SigImage, SenderIPv4, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint tenant lookalike via .com-folding (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com) in phishing URL AIDelivery High
Detects the ARToken redirect trick where the visible anchor shows the vendor's real tenant (mononapfp.sharepoint.com) but the href targets an attacker tenant that folds the vendor's '.com' into the tenant label (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com), inheriting SharePoint's clean reputation. Flags the concrete IOC plus the generic tenant-name-ending-in-'com' folding pattern. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker tenant mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com from the article plus the generalised '.com-folding' regex (tenant label ending in 'com' before .sharepoint.com) that captures the evasion class. Because the destination is still a real sharepoint.com host, reputation-based controls miss it — the tenant-label anomaly is the only reliable signal.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate company whose tenant name genuinely ends in 'com' (e.g. brand called 'Xcom' → xcom.sharepoint.com)
  • Internal users legitimately collaborating with a partner tenant that happens to match the pattern
  • Security-team detonation/sandbox traffic to the lookalike during investigation
  • Safe Links rewrite pre-fetch resolving the domain without a real user click
Suppression filter
| where Name !in~ ("xcom.sharepoint.com") // allowlist known-legit tenants whose label ends in 'com'
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the recipient(s), confirm the tenant label is not a real customer tenant (compare against your SharePoint external-sharing partner list), and pull the source email/anchor text. 2) Contain: block *com.sharepoint.com lookalikes at the proxy/URL filter for the specific tenant, revoke any Safe Links click-through, and force sign-out for users who clicked. 3) Hunt: correlate the resolving hosts to device-code auth (UC3) and any subsequent AAD sign-in from a new IP/device within 30 minutes.
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where UrlDomain endswith ".sharepoint.com"
| where UrlDomain =~ "mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" or UrlDomain matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith ".sharepoint.com"
| where Name =~ "mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" or Name matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code phishing API call: POST /api/device/start with clientMode broker to C2 AIExploitation High
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing exchange on web-proxy telemetry: a POST to /api/device/start against attacker C2 (spx.pamconj.com) carrying the non-standard clientMode:"broker" body used to drive Microsoft's WAM broker flow for MFA-bypass token capture. This is the credential-access request that precedes victim token theft. Rationale: The article documents the exact API contract (POST /api/device/start, clientMode:"broker") matching the Sekoia-documented EvilTokens C2, and names spx.pamconj.com as the C2 host. Path + host together are high-fidelity and platform-specific to this kit. Detection lives on proxy/SWG telemetry (Defender endpoint cannot see the URL path), so defender_kql is intentionally empty; endpoint DNS to the same host is covered by the C2-egress UC.
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app that coincidentally exposes an /api/device/start route on a non-pamconj host (excluded by the host filter)
  • Security research/detonation of the kit from a sanctioned sandbox
  • Proxy log replay/testing
  • URL-scanner pre-fetch of the endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcUsername/SrcIpAddr, confirm the destination is attacker-controlled (spx.pamconj.com / *pamconj.com), and check the user's AAD SigninLogs for a device-code (deviceCode) authentication within minutes. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken / conditional-access session revoke), disable the account if a token was issued, and block *.pamconj.com. 3) Hunt: pivot to the PRT-lifecycle UC for /prt/* calls from the same host and to any new device registration on the account.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/device/start"
| where DstHostname has "pamconj.com" or Url has "pamconj.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens PRT persistence chain: /prt/setup /prt/refresh /prt/renew /prt/reacquire /prt/cookie to C2 AIInstallation High
Hunts the Primary Refresh Token persistence lifecycle that Sekoia flagged as EvilTokens' core differentiator, reproduced in ARToken: web requests to /prt/setup, /prt/refresh, /prt/renew, /prt/reacquire and /prt/cookie against the pamconj.com C2. These calls maintain persistent, MFA-immune access to a compromised Microsoft 365 identity. Rationale: Uses the five named PRT endpoints and the pamconj.com C2 host from the article — the exact persistence chain Sekoia documented for EvilTokens. Requiring the pamconj.com host alongside /prt/* removes any chance of colliding with legitimate internal token services. Path-level signal is proxy-only, so defender_kql is empty by design.
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal identity-service using a /prt/ path on a non-pamconj host (excluded by host filter)
  • Sanctioned red-team emulating EvilTokens PRT flows
  • Proxy log testing/replay
  • Reverse-proxy health checks hitting a /prt/ route on unrelated infrastructure
Response runbook
1) Triage: map SrcUsername to an AAD identity, confirm the C2 host, and review AAD AuditLogs for a 'Register device'/'Add registered owner' event and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs refresh-token reuse for that user. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens, delete any attacker-registered device object, disable the account, and block *.pamconj.com. 3) Hunt: enumerate mailbox inbox-rule creation (forwarding/hiding) and SharePoint file access for the account, and search for other users hitting the same /prt/* C2.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has "pamconj.com" or Url has "pamconj.com"
| where Url has_any ("/prt/setup","/prt/refresh","/prt/renew","/prt/reacquire","/prt/cookie")
| summarize DistinctPrtEndpoints = dcount(Url), Endpoints = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

ARToken Cloudflare Workers lure delivery: {uuid}-docviewer/onedrive/adobe2/document.workers.dev AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint navigation/DNS to the ARToken phishing lure domains served from Cloudflare Workers with the kit's UUID-prefixed themed subdomains (docviewer, onedrive, adobe2, document). These pages host the seven-layer client-side anti-bot gate before delivering the device-code capture flow. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named Cloudflare Workers lure patterns ({uuid}-docviewer/-onedrive/-adobe2.workers.dev) plus the concrete IOC clear90489058903-document.workers.dev. The UUID-prefixed themed subdomain is the kit's fingerprint; the seven-layer anti-bot logic itself lives in the served JS (not in standard logs), so we detect the delivery domain that hosts it.
ATT&CKT1102 T1497 T1027
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers/QA hitting their own *.workers.dev deployments whose subdomain coincidentally contains 'document' or 'onedrive'
  • SaaS products that host document viewers on Cloudflare Workers
  • Security sandbox detonation of the lure
  • URL-scanner/Safe-Links pre-fetch resolving the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-dev") // exclude known developer/CI accounts that deploy to workers.dev
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user, confirm the workers.dev subdomain matches the UUID-prefix + theme fingerprint, and check whether a device-code auth or *.sharepoint.com lookalike followed on the same host. 2) Contain: block the specific workers.dev FQDN (and add a watch for the {uuid}-theme pattern), and warn the user; revoke tokens if auth followed. 3) Hunt: baseline all first-seen *.workers.dev resolutions org-wide (leftanti against 30-day baseline) and correlate to the pamconj.com C2 UCs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)[a-f0-9-]+-(docviewer|onedrive|adobe2|document)\.workers\.dev" or RemoteUrl has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name matches regex @"(?i)[a-f0-9-]+-(docviewer|onedrive|adobe2|document)\.workers\.dev" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint egress to ARToken C2 / phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com, workers.dev) AICommand & Control High
Domain-level net for any host resolving or connecting to ARToken command-and-control infrastructure: the pamconj.com family (pamconj.com, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com) and the known Cloudflare Workers lure clear90489058903-document.workers.dev. This is the catch-all C2/exfil indicator across DNS and network telemetry. Rationale: Uses the article's pre-extracted C2 IOCs verbatim (pamconj.com, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). Fixed the prior validation error by pivoting Sentinel to DnsEvents.Name (a real column) instead of the nonexistent DnsEvents.IPAddresses. Named-domain contact is directly attributable and low-FP.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst or sandbox intentionally resolving the C2 during investigation
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment/validation tooling touching the IOCs
  • Passive-DNS or scanner appliances resolving the domain
  • Sinkholed domain (post-takedown) resolving to a benign park IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" // exclude security tooling and machine-account enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) that made the request and confirm it isn't a sanctioned TI/sandbox tool. 2) Contain: isolate the host if a user browser/Office process initiated it, block *.pamconj.com and the workers.dev FQDN at DNS/proxy, and revoke tokens for any associated user. 3) Hunt: pivot to the device-code (/api/device/start) and PRT (/prt/*) UCs for the same host/user, and sweep the org for other resolvers of pamconj.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "pamconj.com" or RemoteUrl has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith "pamconj.com" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw: risks for the users and how to mitigate them

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-01 3 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Researching OpenClaw vulnerabilities, malicious skills, and other security issues with the popular agent, and providing tips on how to mitigate them.

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected
Phase 2
Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected

Installation
Likely
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files
OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter process (node/python/deno/bun) resolving or connecting to api.telegram.org — the C2/exfil channel used by the malicious ClawHub skill cluster (polymarketbtc family) to ship stolen tokens and crypto keys out. Article-specific because it ties the agent runtime, not a browser, to Telegram Bot API egress. Rationale: api.telegram.org / t.me are the concrete C2 domains for the polymarketbtc ClawHub skill cluster (krajekisbtc) that exfiltrated tokens/keys; scoping the egress to agent interpreters (node/python/deno/bun) rather than browsers is what makes it article-specific and low-noise. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/researchers-find-341-malicious-clawhub.html • https://cofense.com/blog/weaponizing-telegram-bots-how-threat-actors-exfiltrate-credentials • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using a legitimate node/python Telegram bot library for a sanctioned notification bot
  • CI/CD runner posting build status to a corporate Telegram channel via curl
  • Security researcher testing Telegram Bot API integrations in a sandbox
  • Personal productivity script the user knowingly runs that pushes alerts to t.me
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("corp-notify-bot","ci-status") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — identify the skill/script driving the agent and whether the Telegram bot token is hardcoded; correlate to any SKILL.md or config the agent loaded in the prior 10 min. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, rotate all tokens/keys reachable from that host (Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, Slack OAuth, cloud creds, git tokens), and block api.telegram.org egress for non-approved hosts. 3) Hunt: search other hosts for the same agent runtime touching Telegram, and for reads of .env/credentials files by the same runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has "t.me"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "telegram.org" or Name == "t.me"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenClaw Agent Runtime DNS Lookup for Telegram Bot API
id: 6f3a2b1c-9d4e-4c7a-b2f1-8a5e6c0d1e42
description: Detects an agent interpreter resolving Telegram Bot API domains used as a ClawHub malicious-skill exfil channel
references:
  - https://securelist.com/openclaw-security/120484/
  - https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1102.002
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - 'telegram.org'
  selection_tme:
    QueryName: 't.me'
  condition: selection or selection_tme
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:(*telegram.org OR *Telegram.org) OR @DestinationHostname:t.me) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\deno.exe OR *\bun.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/telegram\.org$|^t\.me$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|python|pythonw|deno|bun|curl|powershell)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`

OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter (node/python/deno/bun) spawning a shell whose command line touches secret stores — .env, cloud credential files, SSH keys, .npmrc, or provider API-key variables. Grounded in the article's note that agents keep tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent, which malicious skills harvest via embedded bash. Rationale: The article states agents store tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent and that malicious skills harvest them via embedded bash; scoping parent=agent-runtime + child=shell + a secret-store string in the cmdline is the concrete high-fidelity pivot corroborated by Snyk's OpenClaw credential-leak research. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/openclaw-skills-credential-leaks-research/ • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate skill loading a .env for a sanctioned integration (e.g. a deployment helper reading credentials it is authorized to use)
  • Developer debugging an agent locally and grepping their own .npmrc / .env
  • DevOps automation that echoes an API-key variable name (not value) during setup
  • Package-manager install (npm/pip) that touches .npmrc as part of normal auth
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","pip install") and ProcessCommandLine has ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent agent's loaded skill/config — determine whether the secret access is part of a sanctioned skill or an untrusted ClawHub skill pulled recently. 2) Contain: suspend the agent, quarantine the skill file, and rotate every credential the command referenced (cloud, git, provider API keys, Telegram/Slack tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host+user for outbound connections to api.telegram.org / paste sites shortly after (join to UC1), and sweep other hosts running the same skill hash/name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".env","credentials","id_rsa",".ssh",".npmrc","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (".env","credentials","id_rsa",".ssh",".npmrc","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP + companion APK by SHA256 on endpoints · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP + companion APK by SHA256 on endpoints AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the two Unit 42-published Montana Empire artifacts landing on managed endpoints: the 7,958,528-byte kit ZIP (postal-service brand clone with PHP backend + Telegram C2) and the 12,649,472-byte malicious 'post' APK. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact file hashes rather than any generic phishing behaviour. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 hashes Unit 42 published for the Montana Empire kit ZIP (7,958,528 bytes) and companion [redacted]post.apk (12,649,472 bytes); both hashes were independently confirmed on the origin-unit42 mirror and CyberPress write-up, so they meet the two-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or threat-intel researcher intentionally downloading the sample to a sandbox VM
  • Security team seeding the hash into a detonation/AV-test host
  • Incident-response evidence collection copying the artifact to a forensic share
  • EDR retro-scan re-surfacing a quarantined copy already handled
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARE-SANDBOX-01","IR-FORENSIC-01") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("malware-analyst","threatintel-svc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256, the landing path, and the InitiatingProcess/User that wrote or ran it; verify the host is not a known malware-analysis sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, quarantine/delete the ZIP and APK, and block both hashes org-wide via custom IOC. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process and user to any browser/email download source, look for the kit's PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) or Telegram (api.telegram.org) egress, and check whether the APK was forwarded to other users.
let kitHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
 (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (kitHashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Origin=FileOriginUrl),
 (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (kitHashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, User=AccountName, Origin="")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the Montana Empire kit's distinctive server-side PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) being written to disk or requested over HTTP, indicating the postal-service phishing clone is being staged or is live on infrastructure you can see. Article-specific because these three filenames are the kit's internal component names, not generic web paths. Rationale: Pivots on the three exact PHP component names Unit 42/CyberPress attribute to the Montana Empire kit (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php); these are non-generic internal filenames, so a file-create or IIS request for them is high-fidelity for kit staging on visible infra. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named panel_track.php in an unrelated in-house web app
  • Pen-test / red-team dropping a lookalike phishing kit during an authorised exercise
  • WAF or scanner replaying kit URIs against your site (request hits with 404s, no file on disk)
  • Security researcher unpacking the kit ZIP on an analysis host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the hit is a file-write (kit staged locally) vs an inbound IIS request (external probing); check the folder path, writing process, and HTTP status. 2) Contain: if written to your web root, take the site offline / remove the files and preserve a forensic copy; if inbound-only, block the source IP and confirm no 200 responses. 3) Hunt: look for the kit ZIP hash on the same host, outbound connections to api.telegram.org (kit C2), and any web-shell-style process (php/w3wp spawning cmd/powershell).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| where csUriStem has_any ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the article's core TTP: an AI coding assistant / agent process (Cursor, VS Code+Copilot, Windsurf, Ollama, etc.) making an outbound connection or DNS query to an external domain the org has never seen before — the moment an LLM-hallucinated, adversary-pre-registered 'phantom' domain is fetched with zero reputation. Article-specific because it scopes rare-domain egress to AI-assistant parent processes, the exact trust surface Unit 42 describes. Rationale: No hard domain IOC exists (Unit 42 redacted the live phantom domains and the build-notifier[.]io URL is explicitly illustrative), so this targets the behavioural core of the article — an AI dev-assistant binary reaching a zero-reputation, never-before-seen external domain — via a 30-day leftanti baseline scoped to named AI-client processes. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adopting a new SaaS/API the AI assistant correctly recommended (real, newly-used domain)
  • AI extension auto-update or telemetry endpoint not yet in baseline
  • First use of a new package registry mirror or docs CDN
  • Newly onboarded host with no 30-day baseline generating many first-seen domains
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".github.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".githubcopilot.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".openai.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".anthropic.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".ollama.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".visualstudio.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the first-seen domain's registration age (WHOIS) and reputation; a domain registered within days that matches a brand's naming pattern is the phantom-squat signal, whereas an established SaaS domain is benign. 2) Contain: if the domain is newly-registered/unreputed, block it at DNS/proxy and warn the developer not to hardcode the URL; capture what data the assistant sent. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same domain, check whether the URL was committed into source/config, and review the AI-assistant session for other hallucinated endpoints.
let AiClients = dynamic(["cursor.exe","code.exe","windsurf.exe","ollama.exe","copilot.exe","continue.exe","claude.exe"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same

            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
